utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before returning to evidence, can I mention, I think, three matters in private session because it, in part, relates to confidential material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Somers: [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking to the period of late spring to early summer of 1992, are you aware of any agreements that may have been made between Serbs and Croats in the areas of Katica and Podjele, let's say May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The Serbs wanted to leave Busovaca to go to their own entity, among their own people, and the Serbs made an agreement with the Croats to let them pass so that they could leave unhindered. And in return, in agreement with the officers in charge of the barracks, the Croats would enter the barracks first and the weapons that would be left behind in the barracks would be given to them, as well as their things, their livestock, their entire property. They left all of that to the Croats. And among others, Zdravko Bilanovic left his apartment, or actually he sold some of his things to Franjo Sliskovic, who afterwards married Dario Kordic's sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, the barracks you talked about, that was Sajtovici barracks, are you referring also to the Sajtovici barracks near Koanik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Franjo Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Franjo Sliskovic was an officer, an HVO officer, and he's Anto Sliskovic's brother, Anto being one of the main commanders in Busovaca, and he married the sister of Dario Kordic's wife and he moved into the apartment of Zdravko Bilanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see him in that apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Anto Sliskovic also took an apartment from a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Anto Sliskovic and his wife are living to this day in the apartment of Mico Bulatovic. He left his own apartment that he had been allotted by his company, from the firm he was working in. It was too small for him. Then he moved into this bigger apartment right next to the municipality building, and that is where he is living with his family, the apartment having been owned by Mico Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the Serbs who were leaving the Busovaca municipality required any written permission from the controlling HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They had to request permission from the Croats to leave, because they, all of them, left en masse. No one stayed behind, and they had to have permission, and they were given an escort too by HVO soldiers until they left the territory of Kiseljak, as far as their entity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 25th of January, 1993, what happened, and if you can say what time it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning on the 25th of January at 6.00, the sirens sounded, and we all went into shelters and we hid there. We heard the shooting, detonations, and we took shelter. The closest shelter for me was in a Croat house. My husband, child, and myself, we hid there. We were the only Muslims in that house. The others were Serbs or Croats and their families. However, about 7.00 in the morning, my neighbour ran in and said that they had taken her husband to a camp, and all the other men who had been in the next-door shelter. She was crying. She didn't know what to do. She said, "My husband was there too, and we didn't know what would happen next." As most of the people were Croats in this shelter, they didn't expect any Muslims. In any event, they rounded up all the men, even men under age and elderly men, over 65, and they took them all to the Kaonik prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "rounded up men," of what ethnic group were these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims, Muslims, all the Muslims. They took them to the barracks in Kaonik. In Sajtovici, there was a camp for Muslims, for Muslim men, and they detained them there for several days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband one of the men who was taken to Kaonik and detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was he there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven or eight days, until the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband tell you what he had to do while he was at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was forced to dig trenches at Strane, Loncari, at Kula, at Polje, Ravno, the village of Ravno. He was digging trenches there around the clock. They were mistreated while digging, beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not anyone with your husband or your husband was taken to Katici or Merdani? If you know, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband was not taken to Katici or Merdani, but he did dig at Skradno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many brothers do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have three brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in the shelter with you on the 25th of January? If not, where were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not with me in the shelter. They were near their own house. They were hiding in the attic of a neighbour's, under the roof. That is where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to have contact with them while they were hiding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through relatives, yes. When I went to see them and see how they were doing, all they said was that they were up there, that they were all right, that they were getting food from time to time and so on when there was time to take food up there to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We will return to discussing your brothers in a moment. I would ask for a brief private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to the discussion about your brothers, did they live through the attack -- I'm sorry. Did they survive the incidents in Busovaca? Were they taken prisoner, and if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When my brothers were arrested, one day -- it was sometime at the beginning of February or the end of January -- I came to visit them, and I saw the door leading to the loft had been broken. Something had obviously happened, and a member of the family told me that they had been taken away an hour and a half or two before I had arrived, that they were beaten up right there, that their documents were taken from them, including driving licenses, which were torn up. They were tied up and forced forward. And as they were walking along the street, Anto Sliskovic was personally watching their arrest and overseeing it. And Dragic, who arrested my brother, asked Anto, "What am I going to do with them, Major?" and he said, "Take them there," and they took them away. And as soon as I arrived, I hurried to see what had happened to them, because a member of my family told me that shortly after they had left, she heard a burst of fire and she thought they had been killed. So I went along the road and I met a man, and he told me, "All three Mujahedins are lying in front of the morgue." Along the way, I met Dusko Grubesic. I went up to him and I asked him, "Why have you killed my brothers?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Dusko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Grubesic is the main commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca, and I went up to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... about why he may have killed your brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said to me, "I ordered that not a single Muslim from Busovaca may be killed from now on." And I said, "But Dusko, they had driving licenses with their address in Vitez, because they took their driving test in Vitez, so that the address was indicated on the license plate, and they may have thought they were from Vitez, if you had given orders not to kill people only from Busovaca and it said 'Vitez' on the driving license." And then he said to me, "Wait there," and this was just across the way from the church, "I'll go and check." And he ran up the steps. I didn't have any patience to wait. I ran up after him, and Vlado Cosic was there. They were dialing some numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Vlado Cosic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vlado Cosic was a policeman in the civilian police, and then later he joined the military police. He was in black and he had a white belt, and he was sitting there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you go any further, I want to make sure I understood. What exactly were the words of Dusko Grubesic to your question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said to me, "I have given orders that not a single other Muslim from Busovaca may be killed." And then I explained to him that my brothers' documents had "Vitez" indicated on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you ever come to find your brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Dusko was checking. He called up the police in Kaonik and he couldn't find them, so he was worried too, and he told me to go home and that in an hour's time he would send the police to check where they were. I didn't have any patience to wait, so I went to the civilian police, and the military police was there too and there were military men there. Everyone was there, the military and the civilian police. I asked them for an explanation. They told me that they were not there. Then I went to the morgue to check there, and I came across a friend whom I knew and I asked, "Have my brothers been killed? Are they lying there?" And he told me, "No," that they were someone else, some other people. At the end, they were found at Kaonik. A friend of my brother's told me they had reached Kaonik, and afterwards my brothers told me they had been held for about two hours in the toilet in the bus station, and after that they were transferred to Kaonik. Before going to Kaonik, before they left to Kaonik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, could you please bear in mind that your questions have to directly concern events appearing in the indictment. So will you, please, stick to that, because we cannot, as you know, recount all the events in detail that occurred so long ago. So, please, limit yourself to the things that are directly related to what we are dealing with in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There were two points that had to be made, and I'm afraid they've gotten a little bit gone around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go on to paragraph 15. There's no need to deal with Kaonik or with the 25th of January, about which we've heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. You're satisfied with the Kula digging?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Thank you very much. I'm sorry, which number was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 15; fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a woman named Davorka Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is objected to. I hadn't read it. This is about the accused's sister, yes. It seems to me that it's not relevant, what the accused's sister said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are relationships, I think, that the Court should be made aware of, which I think the names have come before this Court on numerous occasions and I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. The sister, and she's the girlfriend of Pasko Ljubicic, according to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to get that evidence in and just the relationship to the radio station, which I think is important and does go to the persecution counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, speaking for myself, I'm not going to admit the evidence of what the sister said. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask, please, are you familiar with any relationship between, so that we have it in evidence, between Davorka Kordic and Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Davorka Kordic and Pasko Ljubicic for some time had a romantic relationship. They were boy and girlfriend, and it was a big love affair between them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It started sometime before the war, and during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they ever marry, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they never married. At the end, they parted, and he married another girl from Vitez and she married someone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see, on TV Busovaca or any other television station, Dario Kordic and any HVO officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the times briefly that you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them sometime in 1992, June, July, when the HVO troops were taking an oath of allegiance. And Dusko Grubesic lined up his troops belonging to the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, and he saluted to Dario Kordic and offered him his troops to review. And Dario reported back, and Dusko Grubesic reported to him. Kordic saluted back, and Dusko Grubesic reported to Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Kordic [realtime transcript read in error "Dusko Grubesic"] in uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any press conferences at which any HVO officials, other than --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- other than Dario Kordic, or Kordic with other officials, were broadcast on television, and if so, do you recall if any of the content was offensive to any of the Muslim people, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. There's a correction that Ms. Verhaag has indicated. It should be on line 3, 32(3). It's not Dusko Grubesic in uniform. Dario Kordic in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was the question? Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was did you ever witness on television any press conferences in which Kordic, --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- or Kordic in combination with other officials, spoke, and was there any content offensive to the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was happening almost every Tuesday. There was a press centre at Busovaca Television, and it was broadcast on Tuesdays. When journalists -- I don't know which journalists attended. They asked questions, and the propaganda always was that an HVO brigade or soldiers had been attacked by Muslim forces or the Mujahedin, and words like that were used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were always being attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to your husband's situation after his release from Kaonik, after he was exchanged, did he remain at liberty, a free person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. After he was exchanged, he came home, fearing that something could happen to me and the child. He was free for only three days, and then military policemen came to fetch him and took him again to Kaonik, forcing him to dig trenches at Strane, Kula, Loncari, wherever they needed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he sleeping at Kaonik or was it a different type of arrangement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they took him for the first time, he slept at Kaonik for two days. Then he was released home, and he was taken to dig trenches from our house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then after some time, a courier would come with written call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you living in mid-May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was living in my mother's house, because I had been chased out of my apartment. A military policeman came and told me that I had to leave my apartment in five minutes' time, to pick up my personal belongings. I collected some clothes for the child and left, and I asked him, "Where should I go?" And he said, "I don't care where you go." I asked him, "Let me go to Zenica." He said, "You can't, but see where you can go."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you lived in the house where you had been evicted from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1986 until that time when these policemen forced me out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you need permission to live in your mother's house after you were evicted from your house, and if so, who gave you that permission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went because they were evicting people from all houses and they were settling refugees in those houses, people from Stranjani and the surroundings of Zenica, and they were being put up in these houses, the families having been thrown out. And so I feared that would happen to me a second time, so I went to the Sumarija building and asked Dusko Grubesic to give me some kind of certificate so they wouldn't throw me out again. I told him that I had been evicted and that I could be evicted again, and then he gave me a piece of paper saying that I would be safe in my mother's house and that no one would throw me out again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: However --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- excuse me -- to please present Exhibit Z1727.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This document -- I went to Dusko Grubesic, to Sumarija. I found him there upstairs, and he told Dragan Tomacic to write that nobody should disturb me, that I should be safe there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a copy of the document that you were given at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is a copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One quick question about you leaving your own home. Do you know if a Croat family moved in after you were evicted from your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That very moment I left, they took a Croatian family inside. When I came back to pick up some things I had forgotten, the next day, I knocked at the door and asked them whether they would let me take some of the child's things and the photographs, and she said, "No, you can't take anything. I've lost many of my own souvenirs, and you have nothing to look for here."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a woman named Fatima Ibriljic, and if so, how do you know her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. She was living very close by to my house. She was married in Visoko, her husband and son were there, and she came to pick up some documents in January. She was there when the war broke out. She couldn't leave; she was pregnant --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did she want from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She asked me, as I was more familiar with Busovaca and its people, to help her to get out, and I promised that we would go to Frano Kristo to ask him to let her go because she was about to deliver and there was no delivery ward there. So we went to see Frano. Frano agreed to see me and not her. She was crying. On the way, we met Dario Kordic, he was coming out of the church with his two bodyguards and a team of reporters from Radio Television Busovaca. I tried to approach him but his bodyguards wanted to prevent me; however, Dario allowed me to come up to him. I said, "Hello," and I asked, "Where have you been? I can't see you on television and we haven't been seeing you at all," and he said he had been in Novi Travnik and that because of the war he couldn't come to Busovaca for some time. Then I asked him if I could go to Zenica, that I couldn't endure it there anymore, that I had been evicted from my apartment, and he said, "What are you going to do in Zenica? There is starvation there." I said, "Nevermind. I'd like to go. I can't carry on here anymore. You know what's happening here. And if I can't go, could at least Fatima go because she's pregnant?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he helped Fatima. He told me, "Go and see Frano Kristo and tell him that I said that she should be given a permit to leave Busovaca." Then I said, "What if Frano doesn't believe me, because I have already been to see him? He may not believe me that I have seen you," because it was very hard to see him and even harder to talk to him. He said, "If Frano doesn't give it to you, come and look for me." And I asked him, "Where can I find you? Give me your telephone number so I can look for you." Then he told his bodyguard to accompany us to Frano's so that Frano should give Fatima the certificate that she could leave Busovaca, which Frano did. A day or two later, Fatima left with an UNPROFOR ambulance. She was driven to Zenica. But I was not allowed to leave; I stayed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a murder of an individual named Ibro Hodzic in Busovaca in January of 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go to that, can we have a date for this conversation with Mr. Kordic? Can the witness give us a date, roughly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Neslanovic, you've heard the Judge's question. Are you able to give us a month, an approximate month and a year for this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in 1993, I think in July. June or July, roughly about then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to the death of Ibro Hodzic, were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about this event. They were saying that Ibro Hodzic had been killed in his apartment by Dragic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any suspects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They said that Condra had done it. Before that, on the 25th of January, Mirsad Delija had been killed in his house when they were searching Muslim houses allegedly looking for weapons and who knows what else, and Mirsad Delija was then killed in his own house, and then Ibro Hodzic later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's return to Condra. Did you personally ever have any encounters of any type with Condra?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Condra would come across the way to the house where I was living to see some friends who had moved in there from Zenica. He and Dragic, and Cicko, they would gather there. There was a girl that they were all courting, and that is why they would congregate there. Then one day, they were sitting there and joking, and they took my son, who was playing in the yard, they placed him against the wall, and they took a pistol. They were playing around. Anyway, they put him there like a target, and when they fired their pistols, they would hit the facade, sometimes the roof of the house, and then bits of tiles would fall on his head. When the second shot was fired, my son yelled, "Mummy." I heard the shots. I didn't know what was happening. When I came out, I saw my son with his back against the wall, he was terrified. I came up to him, I placed him behind my back, and the person holding the pistol, Cicko, said to me, "I could kill you too without being held to account by anyone." I took the child inside. I just left the house immediately and went to see Branko Sliskovic and told him what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Branko Sliskovic say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told him who did it, and he said, "I'm surprised that Condra Dragic should do that because they are my Anto's escorts." He was surprised that they should be behaving in that way, that they were not with his Anto. They only escorted him -- they would leave Anto only when they went on particular missions; otherwise, they would always be with him. Then he said he would call Anto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, I think we've gone far enough into this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us move on as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may just link up Condra directly through the next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can tell us very quickly, did you go to see Anto Sliskovic, and if so, was he alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After seeing Branko, he told me, "Go and see my Anto. You know where he's working." So I went to his office, Anto's office. I asked his secretary whether I could see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he wasn't alone. Condra was already sitting with him. When I came in to ask whether he could see me, Condra was there, and then Anto refused to receive me. He told me to come some other day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in connection with this story that you were discussing in private session about the Jokers. Were you ever told who commanded the Jokers, and if so, who told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Daro said that he was a Joker, that Pasko Ljubicic was their commander --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Daro the same Darko who you referred to earlier in the private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he was a soldier, that he was getting his salary from Zagreb. I asked him how come he had so much freedom, and he said that he was a special soldier, he was not a front line soldier. He went only on special missions. He differed from the others. He had a higher salary than the others, that his salary was coming from Zagreb, that this special unit was being paid by Zagreb, and they were called the Jokers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Daro tell you who commanded it? I'm afraid I didn't hear your answer earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that Pasko Ljubicic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Daro tell you what types of military actions the Jokers engaged in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he told me that they only went on special assignments, if something had to be taken or reconnoitred, and that they went on special missions and then they would be free again, until the next special assignment. They didn't go to the front, they didn't go to the trenches, that he was a special soldier, he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, why did you come in contact with Daro? What brought you in contact with Daro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a girl there who came from Guca Gora as a refugee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep company with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were no other young girls, she was lonely, so I helped her a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you with her when Daro came to see her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we were together several times when he would come. The two of us would be sitting together and he would join us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these conversations about the Jokers occurred during those times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Tihomir Blaskic in person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain when and with whom, if with anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would see him in the municipality; I would see him with Dario Kordic; I would see him with Kostroman; in the company of Zoran Maric. The leading figures in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he ever in the municipality building where you were working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Anto Valenta in that municipality building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the company of Kordic ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the press centre conferences, on television, they would appear together, and on other occasions too. They were frequently together in Dario's office and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe where Dario Kordic had his offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dario Kordic had his office in the municipality building, then in the post office, in the basement, and at the Ivancica Villa, at Tisovac, in the motel there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he always maintain his office in the municipality building, even when he had other offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you happen to notice, in the time before the attack, the HVO attack, on the 25th of January, in which of these three offices Dario Kordic spent most of his time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the post office and also at Tisovac, but all these places are very close. So in the course of the day, he could visit all three places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not during the war Dario Kordic's family, his wife and children, were living with him in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were living with him in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever notice Dario Kordic to be gone from Busovaca for several days at a time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He wouldn't come to the office, we wouldn't see him; otherwise, we would frequently come across him, and then we would notice his absence of a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to comment on the type of transportation that would be available to HVO persons in Busovaca, particularly HVO officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were jeeps, luxury automobiles, Mercedes, but mostly Land Rovers or jeeps, as we call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, were there any working helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would come too occasionally, not frequently, but two or three times I saw them land at the stadium in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question tying up something you said earlier. When you spoke of Dragic, Condra, and Juka, were they all Croat HVO soldiers, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions. Excuse me. If I could indulge the Court. There was one exhibit that was attached and I didn't realise it was attached to the back of Z1727. If the usher could just point it out to the witness, it is simply a confirmation of her leaving Busovaca, and that would be the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I've made a mistake. I beg your pardon. There was one other exhibit, if the Court would let me just put it in front of the witness. There is also Z175.1. I do apologise. It was buried under my other document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just identify it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on the document in front of you, 175.1, on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Only this part, Kordic, I recognise that that is Dario Kordic's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this document, which is an appointment of certain positions, can you just read into the record what Pasko Ljubicic was appointed to, and nothing more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pasko Ljubicic was appointed to the Civil Defence as an officer. At the time, I was not aware of that because Pasko Ljubicic didn't have an office there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise for having left these out. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just read into the record an exhibit number that has been assigned to those notes which are under seal? The exhibit number is Z1437,3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neslanovic, good afternoon. I'm Mitko Naumovski, a lawyer from Zagreb, and I'm one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Kordic. I will ask you some questions. I should like to ask you not to answer them immediately, to wait for the interpretation of my questions into the languages of the Tribunal. Mrs. Neslanovic, you spoke to the investigators of the Tribunal on three occasions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also make a statement to the state security centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps give a statement to the commission on the establishment of war crimes or some other agency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I gave my statements, but they were from the International Community, and who they were, I suppose they were investigators. That is what they were called, I guess. I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you because all we have are the statements that you gave to the Tribunal investigators and not the other statements that you made to other bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only the Tribunal investigators spoke to me. Those at the state security centre only took me in, but they did not interview me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, very well. Thank you. Let us follow the same order as in your examination-in-chief, but just a few words. We do not think it's particularly material, but this was raised during the chief examination and I have to ask you, that is, something about Mr. Kordic's mother.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can agree that she treated both you and your brothers and other members of your family and that nobody ever complained of her treatment of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she not only treated you during her working hours at the health centre, you also went to her home and she would receive you privately out of friendliness, simply to help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was a physician on duty, and when she would have no patients, she would go home. So she often did the examinations at home, but she worked at the health centre. But then she would go home and she would also receive patients there. That is, if somebody came to look for her at the health centre and she wouldn't be there, then they could go to her home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I meant was that you were a neighbour, so it was quite easy for you. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that she suffered a stroke in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although very many doctors left, she nevertheless had to go on working in 1992 and 1993, and so she did work in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what this document says, 1437,1, that is, that although she was also ill, she tried to take care of everybody in Busovaca as best she could; we agree about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I heard is that she suffered a stroke in 1996, 1997, not before that, that that was the time when she suffered a stroke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. The first one was in 1990, and the second one was in April 1994. That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I didn't know about the first one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last question about that: We shall agree that she was a good physician, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now a few questions relative to your work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you worked from 1997 [sic] and, you say, until January 1993; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you performed your duties throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore in 1992, nobody chased you away from your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but they told me, in 1993, and that is in January 1993, not to come back for work anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nobody forced you to sign any papers in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1992, you even asked for an unpaid leave in addition to your regular annual leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in November 1992, you also did some extra work, and you were rewarded. I think you received 30 per cent of your salary more. You went to clean the office premises, something like that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as the cleaning lady in the municipal hall, you had free access to all the offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, you could also be present at various press conferences that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, those press conferences I watched on television because it was already after the war broke out. There were press conferences before the war too. And I could see them as they came into the municipal hall or came out of the small hall in the -- small room in the municipal hall where they usually held those press conferences or meetings or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we agree that the press conferences took place in the municipal hall, that is, in the meeting room, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe we shall also agree that you personally -- that your movements personally were not constrained. You could go wherever, you could go to the building of the command or the police building or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, no. The police would not allow a neighbour to visit a neighbour or even talk, and they also forbid us to leave our houses. We were told that we were not to leave our houses at all, even though I did not observe that and I just went out of my house because there were things I had to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that is what I asked you. You personally moved about freely around the town, wherever you wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neslanovic, you told us today about an understanding between Serbs who lived in those two villages near Busovaca and the HVO regarding the distribution of weapons at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have no direct knowledge of that, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it from young men who came after the Sajtovici barracks were liberated. When the JNA withdrew from the barracks, then the Territorial Defence, or whatever it was called, the army, was to come there to share the booty with the HVO soldiers. And the HVO soldiers were already in the barracks at the time when they were supposed to enter together, and an armed conflict happened then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we know that. Just a moment. I'm sorry I had to interrupt you. I do understand all that, but the Court has already had an opportunity to hear testimony about the distribution of weapons, and who negotiated with whom, and so on and so forth. But the negotiations were conducted between the delegation of the crisis staff of the Busovaca municipality, including the representatives of both Muslims and Croats, and on the other end the JNA on the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but citizens and in Katici, and they are mostly people of Serb ethnicity, and those soldiers who were already in the barracks and from Podjele and those who lived there, I mean the local people, they were already in the Sajtovici barracks as a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically, do you know that there was a joint Croat and Muslim delegation in Busovaca, during the negotiations which took place at the higher JNA command in Zenica, included a Croat, Florijan Glavocevic, and a Muslim, Asim Sunulahpasic, Zoran Maric, and Besim Spahic, a Muslim who at that time was the mayor of Zenica, that was the delegations, and they were negotiating with the JNA delegation on the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know what was happening here. I don't know what kind of agreement they reached. I know what happened there. When the weapons were to be taken over, a conflict took place because HVO soldiers had already entered the barracks. And Sead Mesic was wounded, and a Muslim fellow who had come there to share those weapons with Croat soldiers withdrew after the JNA withdrew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I don't agree with is your statement that the Croat -- because it was an agreement between the Bosnian Croats on one hand and the JNA on another.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing about the agreement in Zenica. I know about the civilians and the soldiers who were in the barracks who came from Podjele, who went there from the reserve force, those who were in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you already told us that. Since you are mentioning Sunulahpasic was wounded and he's a Muslim, do you know who took him to a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't. I know that he was wounded and he was my neighbour, and he was in the vicinity and we went to pay him a visit. Who took him to the hospital, I don't know. All I know is that he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll refresh your memory by saying that it was Franjo Sliskovic who took him in his car.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But if we're referring to the wounded on that occasion, and the Court has already heard about that, a Croat, Darko Vuleta was wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that Sead was wounded there because he was my neighbour, and that is how I knew that he was wounded, that there had been an armed conflict, so I don't know who else was wounded. I heard about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question on this subject. Do you have any knowledge that apart from the agreement on the distribution of weapons between Croats and Muslims in these barracks in Sajtovici, or rather Kaonik, and that was a local agreement, about 100 Muslims from Zenica arrived and were in front of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honours, I'm not going into that topic anymore. I'm not going to dwell on it, because I believe you have heard a great deal about it already. So let us move on to January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to Kacuni sometime in late January, around the 20th, 21st of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any direct knowledge as to what happened in Kacuni on the 24th of January, 1993, and who was killed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I didn't go there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that it was on that day that the Kacuni-Grabovac road was closed, that one could not drive through Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the road was closed and the roadblocks were reinstituted before that and that the traffic was stopped, but why, I do not know. I know that there were some misunderstandings and that there were some roadblocks there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we agree that these roadblocks were put up by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I mean in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who it was. All I know was that there was a roadblock there and that they were checking who was coming in and who was coming out. But who manned that roadblock, I don't really know, because up there, there was both Croat and Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But whose troops were in Kacuni? Kacuni was the seat of the Territorial Defence or, rather, the barracks of the [indiscernible] Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kacuni, yes, there were troops up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence first and then the army, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Are you aware of another detail relative to this roadblock at Kacuni? Do you know that around the 21st of January, '93, there was an attempt to abduct Ignac Kostroman and Tihomir Blaskic at that roadblock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a few questions about the 25th of January, '93. You, your husband and your son were, you say, in the neighbouring house, in a shelter, together with Croats and Serbs who used to live there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on you say men were taken away to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, the Muslims. Your husband was taken away under somewhat different circumstances than the rest of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The policeman, Josip Maric, was there, and he talked to your husband about that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was Josip Maric who told your husband that they had come to take him to prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. To a separate place, to a safer place, and it was called prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was that Croat policeman who also said to your husband the following, and I'm quoting: "It is up to you to say whether you want to stay here or come with us, but it will be safer for you if you came with us because somebody who does not know you might kill you?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was safer for him to be in the prison than to stay free, that is, at home, for instance, because there anyone could kill him. So that there, there in the camp, the chances were better that he would keep his life than if he were free in the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The final question about that. Your husband decided himself to go with them, I mean, it was of his own free will, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he said, "Well, if it's safer there, then I'll go there, if you can guarantee that nothing will happen to me there," and he guaranteed that nothing would happen to him there, that he would take care of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So your husband spent some seven or eight days at Kaonik, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he wasn't beaten, he wasn't harassed by anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not beaten because they knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more thing about your husband. You said that when he came home, he had to go and dig trenches wherever it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said today, and the Prosecutor interrupted you, that he received a summons in writing to report to a place where he was to dig.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, they would come after him. Later on, they would send a written summons that at such and such a time he should go and dig trenches at such and such a place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it who brought those summons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a young man, rather, a man of Muslim ethnicity --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked at the municipal hall, and you more or less knew the organisation, which department existed, so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can agree, I suppose, that in the former state and also in the present state, Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia, there was an institution called the civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when your husband went to dig trenches, who was the chief of the civil defence in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Viktor Maric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose you also know who were bound by that kind of duty. Who were people who were bound to dish out certain duties within the civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Practically all citizens who were not militarily-able were dished out various duties in the civilian defence, and my husband was militarily-able; that is, all of them, including women and children, all those who could help, for instance, rescue somebody from the ruins, put out a fire, so on and so forth; that is, all those citizens who could move around and were not militarily-able, were not of military age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can agree that your husband would receive summons signed by Viktor Maric, who was the chief of the civil defence in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was his labour obligation, in a way, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, a few questions about your brothers, and there is no need to mention their names. You said that you had three brothers. Were your brothers members of the Territorial Defence of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were members of that particular Busovaca detachment, as it was called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you speak up a bit, please, because I'm afraid the interpreters can't hear you properly. Thank you. Your brothers were at Kadica Strana on the 24th and 25th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not. They were at home. That was somebody else. It's not far off, but it's a different street. They were at their own home. On that particular day, I happened to have been with them. On the 24th, I was at their place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave their house on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left before dark, perhaps it was 6.00 or 7.00 p.m., thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally have no knowledge as to where your brothers were on the night between the 24th and 25th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they were at home. They were safeguarding their house because their families were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke today about the arrest of your brother several days later, but I noticed that in none of the previous statements did you make mention of one particular detail, that Anto Sliskovic supervised their arrest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention that because it was a long period of time and I had to try and remember each detail, and my brother told me that later on and he referred to him as captain, what are you doing with them, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did your brother tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my brother told me that after the arrest. When I go back and remember all those details and think about it, and then he said that Anto had personally supervised his arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is only something that you heard later on; you don't know it directly yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned today that the wrong conclusion was made that your brothers had been killed and that you then looked for them all over Busovaca, and in addition to that, you contacted Dusko Grubesic to ask him about it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he was the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, but you did not say where the brigade's headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Dusko personally was at his headquarters, that's where he had his offices, in the Sumarija building on the ground floor, where the TO offices had previously been located. The brigade, that is to say, their brigade, had their offices at the stadium and in the primary school building and in the barracks as well and in the Udruga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the headquarters was in the Sumarija building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Dusko was in the Sumarija building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I have understood you correctly, and from your previous statements and from what you said today, Dusko Grubesic made a great deal of effort to locate your brothers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he undertook -- he checked up on them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said today, when you talked to him about the fear you had for your brothers, that he told you, that is to say, that Dusko Grubesic, commander of the Busovaca Brigade, told you that he had issued an order that no single Muslim in Busovaca would be killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Must not be killed. He used the word "must." "Not a single Muslim must be killed anymore in Busovaca," that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and I noticed that you used that word, "must not be any Muslim killed," but I have in front of me notes from your conversation with the investigator, dated the 31st of September, 1997, and at the end, the translator, the interpreter says that these notes represent the verbatim record of your conversation with the investigator. In that particular statement, and we just have the English version in front of us, on page 5, the last paragraph, in that paragraph, you told the investigator that Dusko Grubesic said the following: "Don't worry. I have issued an order that not a single man in Busovaca will be killed anymore."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He said, "No single Muslim must be killed," that's what he said, because it was only the Muslims that were killed at the time because the conflict was between the Muslims and the Croats. And he told me, "I ordered that not a single Muslim must be killed anymore," that no Muslims should be killed anymore -- must be killed anymore, although there had been quite a few of them who had been killed before that. And several days elapsed, and then he said that he had ordered this. He didn't tell me who he had ordered it -- who he had issued the orders to, but he said that not a single other Muslim may be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, the Chamber has heard in the examination-in-chief this quote, so there's no point in going back to that. We have already heard it, that not a single Muslim may be killed. So let us move forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to point out the difference in the previous statement because the Muslims are not mentioned in the previous statement. It makes reference to "anybody," so that was my reaction. But if you say that we have exhausted that point, I can move forward, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may, please, just comment that what Mr. Naumovski is reading from is not a statement at all signed by the witness. It is simply what is called "Witness Information" taken by investigators. So this is not ratified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to my learned friend for that assistance. I have just made that point myself. Thank you. We may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you found your brothers, thank God, safe and sound. They were in Kaonik and they were released later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they had been beaten up and mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were released on the 8th of February when the exchange took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now have a few questions with respect to when you left your house. You described the circumstances under which you were forced to leave here today, and now I should like to ask you whether you agree with me when I say that from 1992, ever since the war began in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that several large groups of refugees and displaced persons had come into Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was a large group of refugees from the Jajce area in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was also a very large group made up of the inhabitants, that is to say, Croats from Travnik and the surrounding villages, Guca Gora, Slanja, and all that area, and in the summer of 1993, they came, and a figure of 18.000 is mentioned, which means a great influx of refugees to the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the exact number of those refugees, but there were a considerable number. That was where their centre was, and some of them stayed there. Others went off, depending on how they found accommodation and lodging and anything else. People who were not satisfied with the accommodation they got there, they would go further on and look for other accommodation elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were forced to leave your house, some refugees took up residence in your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a detail today that when you came to look for your things the next day, that the refugees said, "Unfortunately, madam, we had to leave all our memories behind." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, you lived for a time in your mother's house. I don't want to take too much time on that point, but what is important is Z1227, that is to say, that you asked the commander of the Busovaca Brigade, Dusko Grubesic, to issue a certificate to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to protect me in some way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to the Sumarija building, to the command headquarters there, and you were issued that certificate there, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It speaks for itself, but basically it said that nobody must trouble you in the house in which you were living, that is to say, in your mother's house, that you would be protected there. You told us that you tried to leave Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You asked UNPROFOR to help you leave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I asked the authorities in the police. Frano was there, Frano Kristo, first of all, I asked him, and he told me that I was to go to UNPROFOR, and "if UNPROFOR gives you a certificate that they would be taking you out, then we shall also issue you a certificate giving you permission to leave." Then I went to UNPROFOR to ask them whether they would be willing to issue me a certificate to leave Busovaca, and they told me that Zenica had accused them of performing ethnic cleansing, if they were to export or allow Muslims to leave under pressure of any kind. So they told me that they were accused of performing ethnical cleansing by Zenica and so they refused to take me out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about Frano Kristo, you just said that he was chief of police, but he was chief of the civilian police, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, although there was the army there as well. There was the army and the police. So I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was in the civilian police, I think you agree with that, and that's what you said in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but he did not have the authority to issue orders to let me go. He had to ask Anto Sliskovic or some of the other soldiers who made the decision, so he had to ask them first whether to allow me to leave, which means, that as a civil policeman, he did not decide on the fates of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a detail which I omitted a moment ago when the witness spoke about UNPROFOR and the assistance to leave and Muslims to leave, Witness Sepa spoke about that subject, and that is the detail that I wish to bring up. He mentioned services in the form of transport because he was stationed in Busovaca. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to emphasise that he was in the civilian police force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You received another certificate, apart from the one that Dusko Grubesic gave you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I received a certificate when I was to leave Busovaca. First of all, Nikica Petrovic called me and had a talk with me and said, well, he would allow me and my child to leave, to go to Zenica, and he ordered Frano to give me a written statement or certificate giving me free passage to leave Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had in mind another certificate. Did you receive a certificate, that is to say, you did receive a certificate, I think, signed by Zoran Maric, which also stated that nobody was allowed to interfere with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I received a certificate of that kind, that nobody must molest us, all those who were left in Busovaca, that we were not allowed -- nobody was to expel us from our homes. But it was quiet for two or three days after that, and afterwards, that paper meant nothing because they carried on what they were doing before that. So that paper was, in fact, worthless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I have several questions to ask you. You worked in the municipality, did you not, so you know things about that. Let me ask you about the power structure, so to speak, in the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Florijan Glavocevic was the president of the HVO up until August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that Florijan Glavocevic was the president of the municipality. I did not know that he was president of, as you say, the representative of the HVO. I didn't know that. I just knew that he was the president of the municipality and that he worked as such in the Busovaca municipality. But what function he had or post he had in the HVO, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just check. Are we speaking of the same period, the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Later on, the function performed by Glavocevic was taken over by Mr. Maric; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before Florijan, I think Zoran was before Florijan. I don't recall exactly. There was Niko Grubesic, there was Florijan Glavocevic, and then Zoran Maric, and they were all presidents at a similar time, but I don't mow who was the first, second, or third. I think that Niko Grubesic came after Florijan, and before that, I think it was Zoran Maric, something of that kind. That's how it must have been because Zoran Maric was there in 1992 or -- well, yes, there was a -- I think it was Florijan and then Niko Grubesic replaced him. But all three of them were presidents of the municipality, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Niko Grubesic, in fact, came after the war, that he was the mayor of Busovaca afterwards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the period that I'm referring to, Mr. Niko Grubesic was the secretary of the municipality. I think that's what you called him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was in 1992. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume that you know some of the details related to the military organisation of the HVO in Busovaca. Ivo Brnada was the commander of the HVO in May 1992; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the first commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know there was Dusko, and then due to illness, he had to leave to Split and he was replaced during that time by Jure -- I don't remember his surname, Jure Cavara, and then once again, Dusko came back. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know who was there before him in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only know the time when Dusko was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall, with greater precision, when he was the commander in the framework of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in 1992, the summer of 1992. I met him sometime in April. He was in Split but had come back from Split because he had some lung problems. He was ill, but he was the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to tell me more exactly whether you know when the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade was formed in Busovaca in more precise terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I just have one more question related to your personal status. You explained to us a moment ago that you were given permission to leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were, in fact, exchanged -- that is, there was a personal exchange that took place. Your husband found a family in Zenica, a Croat, and then you were exchanged that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only way in which I was able to leave Busovaca, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us in your statement, in one of your statements, that many families were exchanged privately, so to speak, in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My husband was in Zenica and the other person's husband was in Busovaca, and so they would exchange families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Neslanovic, I have several questions to ask you with regard to your acquaintance with Fatima Ibriljic, who was pregnant at the time. You tried to help her, and you went to the civilian police to talk to Frano Kristo, whether that woman would be allowed to leave, permitted to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kristo promised that he would see what he could do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would only see what he could do about me. He would talk to Anto Sliskovic, because he was in charge of civilians, and that he had to have agreement from Anto Sliskovic to allow me to leave. And then I mentioned Fatima, and he said, well, he would do that next time. So he made no promises with regard to letting Fatima leave, that he would promise to talk to Anto Sliskovic about me, what he could do to have me leave. So I went to Frano on several occasions, asking him to give me permission to leave. He would just say, "Well, find Anto Sliskovic. He's the main man, he's the man in charge, and if he says you can go, then you can go."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's stick to the topic in hand. I'd now like to ask you a few details about this particular lady. On that same day when you went to the police station to talk to Frano Kristo, you met Mr. Kordic, who was coming out of the church or somewhere like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We agree, I think, that Mr. Kordic was friendly towards you and told the escort to let you go by, and you said a few -- exchanged a few friendly words there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point, this pregnant lady with tears in her eyes came up to you and told you about her own personal problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, she was crying, so I explained her predicament. She wasn't able to say anything, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You asked Mr. Kordic, in friendly terms, to help the woman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic promised that he would help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He said he would contact the chief of the civilian police, that is to say, Frano --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he told me to tell Frano that he had said that Fatima should be given permission to leave Busovaca, and I had just come from Frano Kristo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you've described that to us already, thank you, not to waste time. The next thing I want to ask you is this: Mr. Kordic promised to help and sent one of his escorts to accompany that pregnant lady to the civilian police station to see what could be done; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not in the office when they talked to Frano Kristo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's correct. I waited outside. In fact, the escort wouldn't allow me to enter. I wanted to go in, but he wouldn't let me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
